title: India Positions Itself to Lead the Global Sustainable Aviation Fuel Market
excerpt: With CORSIA Phase II approaching and Akasa Air-BPCL signing an SAF partnership, India is building the infrastructure and policy framework to become a major player in the $15 billion green aviation fuel industry.
body:
Key Takeaways
  • India aims for 1% SAF blending by 2027, increasing to 5% by 2030.
  • Akasa Air and BPCL's MoU marks a significant step in India's SAF development.
  • India's aviation market is set to double to 500 million passengers by 2030.
  • SAF-blended jet fuel use is officially permitted starting April 2026.

  • India has set SAF blending targets of 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030, aligning with ICAO's CORSIA mandate for reducing aviation emissions.
  • Akasa Air and BPCL signed an MoU to collaborate on SAF supply at designated airports across India, marking a concrete industry step.
  • India's abundant biomass resources and growing aviation market — set to double to 500 million passengers by 2030 — position it as a natural SAF production hub.
  • The Ministry of Petroleum officially permitted SAF-blended jet fuel use in April 2026, removing a key regulatory barrier.

The Opportunity

India sits at the intersection of two powerful trends: it is the world's third-largest aviation market with passenger traffic projected to double to 500 million by 2030, and it possesses roughly 230 million tonnes of surplus agricultural residue — exactly the kind of feedstock needed to produce sustainable aviation fuel at scale.

That combination has put India at the centre of a global conversation about who will dominate the emerging SAF market as mandatory emission offsetting under ICAO's Carbon Offsetting and Reduction Scheme for International Aviation (CORSIA) takes effect in 2027.

> **"The EU requires 2% SAF blending by 2025 and up to 70% by 2050."**

Policy Framework Takes Shape

The Indian government has moved quickly to build the regulatory architecture. In April 2026, the Ministry of Petroleum officially permitted the use of Aviation Turbine Fuel blended with SAF, amending the ATF Marketing Order to expand the fuel's definition. The Ministry of Civil Aviation, in partnership with ICAO and the European Union, released a detailed SAF Feasibility Study that charts a production roadmap tailored to India's specific feedstock availability and infrastructure readiness.

Blending targets have been set at 1% by 2027, 2% by 2028 and 5% by 2030. Civil Aviation Minister Ram Mohan Naidu has described SAF as central to India's sustainable aviation strategy, reaffirming the country's ambition to achieve self-sufficiency in SAF production.

Industry Moves From Talk to Action

The Akasa Air-BPCL partnership, announced on July 15, represents one of the first concrete commercial agreements in India's SAF ecosystem. The MoU establishes a framework for SAF-blended fuel supply at designated airports, with both companies sharing demand forecasts and supporting a phased increase in blending as domestic production matures.

Key Partnerships in SAF
›Akasa Air and BPCL signed an MoU for SAF supply.
›NTPC Green Energy is negotiating with major airlines.
›Airbus advocates for SAF investments under CSR.
›SAF could create 1.1 to 1.4 million jobs.

They are not alone. NTPC Green Energy is in discussions with global carriers including British Airways, Lufthansa, Singapore Airlines and Virgin Atlantic to supply SAF from its green hydrogen hub in Andhra Pradesh. Airbus has called for SAF investments to qualify under India's Corporate Social Responsibility mandate, arguing the industry could create 1.1 to 1.4 million jobs.

Global Competitive Landscape

India is entering a crowded field. The EU requires 2% SAF blending by 2025 and up to 70% by 2050. The US, UK, Japan and Singapore have each set their own targets. But India's advantages are structural: deep agricultural waste availability, a large and growing domestic aviation market that provides built-in demand, and a technology talent pool capable of scaling complex production pathways.

The challenge remains price. Industry estimates put SAF at two to four times the cost of conventional jet fuel. Bridging that gap will require production scale, policy incentives and international cooperation — areas where India's government has signalled clear intent but where execution will determine whether ambition translates into market dominance.

What to Watch

The next milestone is CORSIA Phase II in 2027, when mandatory emission offsetting begins for international flights. Indian carriers that can demonstrate SAF usage will face lower offsetting requirements, creating a direct commercial incentive. The country's success in meeting its own blending targets — and attracting the investment needed to build production capacity — will determine whether India becomes a SAF exporter or remains dependent on imports for a fuel it has the raw materials to produce domestically.
